claims.text: Routine infant HIV testing includes multiple entry points, specifically nutrition, inpatient, and TB clinics.
In generalized epidemic settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status should be offered HIV testing in outpatient and immunization clinics.
For infants or children presenting with unknown exposure, the process involves assessing for HIV exposure (such as performing antibody testing on the mother if her status is not known).

Even if HIV exposure is not recorded, a NAT test should be performed for any HIV-exposed child who presents outside of the national infant testing algorithm with clinical symptoms, irrespective of previous NAT results.

results.question: A malnourished child is admitted to the ward and nobody knows their HIV status. Should they be tested?

claims.text: HIV testing services should not only be clinic-based; community-based HIV testing outside health facilities is a recognized entry point and includes outreach, community-based services, workplaces, clubs, bars, places of worship, and educational establishments.

Additional testing delivery approaches outside health facilities include mobile testing (such as through vans or temporary testing facilities), community voluntary counselling and testing centres, and HIV self-testing offered in the community.

results.question: Is clinic-based HIV testing enough, or should testing also be offered outside health facilities?

claims.text: In generalized epidemic settings, infants and children with unknown HIV status should be offered HIV testing in outpatient and immunization clinics.
HIV testing for infants and children may be integrated with other health services, such as immunization or nutrition counselling.

results.question: Should immunization and outpatient clinics be offering HIV tests to children who have never been tested?

claims.text: An infant or child's HIV exposure is determined by checking whether the child had HIV exposure through the mother.
Exposure status is classified as unknown if the mother's HIV status is unknown, not exposed if the child is not known to have been exposed to HIV, or HIV-exposed.

results.question: How do I find out whether a nine-month-old was exposed to HIV?

claims.text: For children after 18 months of age (which includes a two-year-old), serology testing and the national HIV testing algorithm should be used for diagnosis.
The specific test to use depends on national policies and considerations such as facility test availability.

claims.text: For any client with an HIV-positive test result, providers should offer or refer for support for disclosure and partner services.
Post-test counselling should ensure confidentiality and discuss the benefits and risks of disclosing HIV-positive status to partners, while supporting individuals with disclosure.
Planning for disclosure should include steps to maximize the client's physical safety and discuss voluntary disclosure and partner services options.

claims.text: For infants and children younger than 18 months of age, nucleic acid testing (NAT) / virological testing should be performed to diagnose or confirm HIV infection.
Same-day point-of-care NAT should be considered and prioritized for infant diagnosis at all relevant time points to maximize clinical benefits and linkage to care.
If a mother tests HIV-positive, NAT should be performed on the HIV-exposed infant across various time points (such as birth testing where of value, at six weeks, and at nine months).

When the preferred option is not used, ATV/r, DRV/r, LPV/r, or RAL may be considered as alternative third drug options for PEP when available.
NVP should not be used for PEP in adults, adolescents, and older children due to the risk of life-threatening serious adverse events.

claims.text: For neonates (age < 4 weeks) who are first-time ART users, the preferred first-line ART regimen is either AZT + 3TC + RAL or ABC + 3TC + RAL.
Neonates who start ART on a RAL-based regimen should transition to DTG as soon as possible.
Due to limited availability of ABC syrup, AZT syrup remains an effective option to combine with 3TC during the first 4 weeks of life.

claims.text: Third-line ART regimens are not specifically defined by WHO, and national programmes are advised to develop policies for third-line ART.
Third-line regimens should include new drugs with minimal risk of cross-resistance to previously used regimens, such as INSTIs and second-generation NNRTIs and protease inhibitors (PIs).
Patients on a failing second-line regimen who have no new ARV options available should continue on a tolerated regimen.

claims.text: Under the package of care algorithm for people with advanced HIV disease, patients who test positive for TB start TB treatment and also start co-trimoxazole prophylaxis according to WHO recommendations.

Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for adults, adolescents, and children with HIV who have a CD4 cell count <350 cells/mm³, clinical stage 3 or 4 disease, or any CD4 count in settings with a high prevalence of malaria or severe bacterial infections.

Co-trimoxazole chemoprophylaxis is generally recommended to prevent Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia and other coinfections for individuals with an HIV-positive test result and clients receiving HIV care.

claims.text: In infants and children living with HIV, symptoms that should prompt evaluation for TB include cough (or current cough), fever (or fever of 39 °C or greater), and poor weight gain or weight loss.
In young children, symptom screening should also include reduced playfulness or lethargy, and cough may be absent.

claims.text: In the 'Treat All' era, all individuals diagnosed with HIV should be rapidly initiated on ART to optimize treatment outcomes and prevent new infections.

Individuals should not be coerced into starting ART immediately and must be supported to make an informed choice regarding when to start treatment, as some people need time to adjust to their diagnosis.
Retesting to verify HIV status must be performed prior to starting ART.
Follow-up should be arranged for clients who are unable to enrol in HIV care on the day of diagnosis.
Monitoring quality of care and linkage intervals disaggregates ART initiation timing based on national guidelines (such as within 7, 28, 30, or 90 days of diagnosis).
